mechanism.attack: The mechanism chain asserts shell-wall strain maps cleanly to localized differential foundation settlement. A welded steel tank shell on a granular pad is not a simply-supported plate; under differential settlement, the shell redistributes load through hoop stress redistribution, membrane buckling, and bottom-plate flexure, and a substantial fraction of the foundation settlement is accommodated by the bottom plate and annular region without producing measurable strain in the courses above. Industry data on tank settlement observation (e.g., API 653 settlement profiles) show that shell-course strain at 2 m pitch is dominated by global "out-of-plumb" tilt and thermal gradients, not by localized differential pad compression. The 1.2 pm/microstrain sensitivity is fine in a lab coupon, but here the actual transfer function epsilon_settle = E_corr/L_span assumes the shell acts as a Euler-Bernoulli beam between settlement points — which it does not, because the bottom two courses are constrained by the bottom-plate weld and by the chime, and because membrane action in the cylindrical shell couples azimuthal and vertical strain. The 5 mm/m differential settlement claim implies microstrain levels comparable to or below the daily thermal strain envelope, even after the cited 6-13 microstrain/°C compensation; "co-located reference gratings" on the same shell cannot isolate solar/shading differentials along the 2 m vertical pitch, so the compensated signal is dominated by differential thermal expansion of the shell, not settlement.
mechanism.basis: The equation epsilon_settle = E_corr/L_span treats the shell as a 1D beam between settlement points, violating cylindrical-shell membrane theory (Donnell-Mushtari); in a real tank the bottom two courses are boundary-fixed by the bottom-plate weld so vertical bending strain from pad settlement is suppressed and replaced by hoop/bending coupling. Combined with the cited [cal:kg02:r2] thermal cross-sensitivity of 6-13 microstrain/°C being larger than the predicted settlement signal, the signal-of-interest cannot be discriminated from the noise floor using co-located references on a shell that experiences 10-20°C diurnal gradients at the 2 m vertical pitch.

physics.attack: The Bragg grating itself is physically sound (~1.2 pm/microstrain at 1550 nm is correct for silica fiber). The physical flaw is not in the grating but in the assumption that a wavelength shift on a fiber bonded to the OUTSIDE of a shell in thermal equilibrium with the shell faithfully reports localized foundation settlement. Three concrete physics problems: (1) The FBG is bonded to the outer shell surface, typically under a coating system, while the inner surface sees product at temperature; the through-thickness thermal gradient creates bending strain that is indistinguishable from the settlement strain. (2) At the bottom two courses, the shell is effectively rigidly connected to the bottom plate; any differential settlement is accommodated by elastic deformation concentrated within ~0.5 m of the chime, not distributed over the 2 m grid pitch. (3) Long-term creep and stress relaxation in the adhesive bond (epoxy or weld pad) will rebaseline the grating and mimic or mask settlement.
physics.basis: Through-thickness thermal gradient on a sun-exposed steel shell with internal product at a different temperature produces bending strains on the order of several microstrain per °C of differential; this is the same order as [cal:kg02:r2]'s cited 6-13 microstrain/°C, and it cannot be removed by co-located references because the references experience the same gradient. Adhesive creep on outdoor FBG bonds is documented to drift several microstrain/month, exceeding the settlement signal.

evidence.attack: The cited records [cal:kg02:r1] and [cal:kg02:r2] are truncated mid-sentence ("...field deployments on b" and "...measured cross-sensitivity 6-13"). The evidence does not demonstrate (a) deployment on a storage tank shell, (b) detection of localized differential settlement, or (c) long-term stability under tank-farm conditions (UV, coating chemistry, product vapor, thermal cycling). The 1.2 pm/microstrain number is a well-known bulk fiber coefficient; nothing in the cited evidence ties it to bonded-on-tank-shell performance, which is degraded by shear-lag, adhesive modulus, and coating compliance. The "5 mm/m within 7 days at 99% confidence" claim has no cited provenance.
evidence.basis: Both evidence records are truncated and lack the deployment context (tank shell, settlement detection, long-term stability) that the mechanism claims; [cal:kg02:r1] ends mid-word and [cal:kg02:r2] ends with "6-13" with no units, no period, no outcome. No record supports the 5 mm/m / 7 days / 99% confidence specification.

prior_art.attack: [cal:kg02:pa1] discloses FBG strain monitoring on civil infrastructure including bridges and dams — the same sensor modality (FBG + bonded strain transfer) applied to detect mechanical deformation in steel/concrete structural elements. While [cal:kg02:pa1] is not on a tank shell specifically, the mechanism (bonded FBG → strain → deformation inference) is identical, so the candidate cannot claim novelty of mechanism. More damaging is [cal:kg02:pa2]: inclinometer-based settlement arrays ALREADY monitor tank-foundation settlement externally with documented resolution, and are accepted under API 653 inspection practice. intervention.attack: The intervention specifies "8 rings × 8 azimuths" per tank = 64 gratings, "lowest two shell courses," and one tunable-laser scanner shared across the farm. Concrete engineering problems: (1) Bonding 64 FBGs through the tank's external coating requires coating removal, FBG installation, and recoating at every grid point — this is a major hot-work/coating-disruption activity that on a large tank triggers API 653 confined-space and hot-work permitting, plus recoating QA per the tank's coating specification. The cost of installation approaches the cost of an out-of-service settlement survey. (2) Sharing one scanner across N tanks via optical switching introduces scan-time multiplexing: each tank is interrogated at 1/N of the duty cycle, degrading SNR by sqrt(N) and lengthening detection latency well beyond the 7-day claim for farms with more than a few tanks. (3) The "lowest two shell courses" are the most corrosion-prone and the most likely to be replaced/repaired during the 5-8 year window, destroying the sensor grid.
intervention.basis: Coating removal/reapplication on 64 points per tank on the bottom two courses (the highest-maintenance courses, per API 653 corrosion inspection records) is operationally prohibitive; the 7-day detection latency cannot be achieved with a single shared scanner across a typical farm of 10-50 tanks at realistic scan rates of ~1 Hz per channel.

predicted_effect.attack: "Detection of differential settlement > 5 mm/m within 7 days of onset at 99% confidence" is unsupported by the evidence base and contradicted by the thermal noise floor. 5 mm/m of differential settlement over a chord of, say, 4 m (two azimuthal sensors apart at ~4 m arc length) corresponds to ~1.25 mm of vertical displacement difference, producing shell bending strains on the order of tens of microstrain in a simply-supported plate model — but in a real tank with bottom-plate fixity, much of this is absorbed at the chime. Even granting the higher strain estimate, the detection must occur above 3-sigma thermal noise. With [cal:kg02:r2]'s 6-13 microstrain/°C cross-sensitivity and typical 5-10°C diurnal swings on a partially-filled or sun-exposed shell, the 3-sigma noise floor is on the order of 30-60 microstrain peak-to-peak — comparable to or larger than the settlement signal. The 99% confidence claim has no statistical basis in the cited evidence.
predicted_effect.basis: 99% confidence within 7 days requires the settlement signal to exceed 3-sigma of the compensated noise floor; with cited cross-sensitivity of 6-13 microstrain/°C and realistic 5°C residual thermal gradient after reference compensation, noise is ~30-60 microstrain, while the settlement signal in a bottom-plate-fixed shell is at most tens of microstrain. Detection is not statistically distinguishable.

experiment_design.attack: The killer experiment — hydraulic jacks under one quadrant in 2 mm steps to 10 mm on a "test tank" — is a single-event, short-duration laboratory exercise that cannot validate the field failure modes that would kill this candidate: (1) long-term adhesive creep over the 3-8 year interval; (2) thermal gradient effects from solar loading and product temperature; (3) coating-system compatibility and survival; (4) noise floor under real ambient conditions; (5) the bottom-plate fixity that suppresses the very signal being measured. A short jack test on an empty, freshly-prepared test tank will produce large, clean signals that have no bearing on field performance under operational conditions. The kill condition (>6 mm/m above 3-sigma thermal noise in 7 days) is also poorly specified because "thermal noise" is not defined operationally.
experiment_design.basis: The jack test does not exercise the dominant field failure modes (adhesive creep, thermal gradients through the shell wall, coating compliance, bottom-plate membrane action) and therefore cannot kill the mechanism in the conditions where the candidate is actually deployed. The kill threshold "3-sigma thermal noise" is undefined and unmeasurable in the proposed test.

boundary_conditions.attack: The boundary conditions acknowledge thermal compensation is required and that this is not a corrosion replacement. However, they understate the thermal problem: "co-located reference gratings" cannot cancel the through-thickness thermal gradient because both the measurement and reference gratings sit on the same (outer) surface. They also omit: (1) vapor/atmospheric corrosion of the bonding pads in a tank-farm environment (H2S, hydrocarbon vapor); (2) mechanical damage risk from external activity (lawnmowers, vehicles, livestock on small terminals); (3) lightning and electrical surge vulnerability of the long fiber runs from tank to shared scanner; (4) the requirement to enter confined space to bond gratings on the bottom two courses; (5) the requirement to remove and reinstall the tank's external coating system with full QA per the original coating spec.
boundary_conditions.basis: Co-located references on the same shell surface experience the same through-thickness thermal gradient as the measurement gratings and therefore cannot cancel the dominant thermal noise; this is a geometric/fundamental limitation, not an engineering detail.

attack.final_objection: KILLED, on the basis that the cited thermal cross-sensitivity ([cal:kg02:r2]: 6-13 microstrain/°C) exceeds the predicted settlement signal in a real tank with bottom-plate fixity and non-uniform shell thermal loading, making the specified 5 mm/m / 7 days / 99% confidence detection physically unachievable regardless of grid density or scanner quality.

mechanism.attack: The mechanism claims that splitting the prefractionation and main sections into one shell eliminates "remixing entropy penalty." This conflates two distinct phenomena. In a direct two-column sequence separating a close-boiling binary (relative volatility 1.15), there is no ternary middle-boiling component to distribute — only two products. The classic dividing-wall advantage requires a TERNARY feed where the middle component can be withdrawn as a sidestream without remixing. Here α=1.15 between two components is a binary split dressed as a ternary. The "remixing term" referenced in the Underwood-Gilliland framework does not exist for a binary direct sequence; it is a finite ternary phenomenon. The mechanism as stated does not produce the predicted 27-32% duty reduction for a binary close-boiling split.
mechanism.basis: Dividing-wall columns save energy by avoiding the remixing of a middle-boiling component in a TERNARY separation (e.g., Kaibel, Petlyuk configurations). A binary split with α=1.15 produces only distillate and bottoms; no intermediate sidestream exists to "remix." The stated mechanism requires a ternary or pseudo-ternary feed that is not established in the problem statement.

physics.attack: Even if we grant pseudo-ternary behavior (e.g., light impurity, target A, heavy B with the impurity acting as a "middle"), the 27-32% duty reduction band cited from cal:kg03:r1 applies to separations where the middle-boiling fraction is substantial (typically 20-40% of feed). For trace or near-trace middle components in a dominant binary split, the duty savings collapse toward single-digit percentages because the prefractionator section becomes thermodynamically trivial. The candidate gives no feed composition, so the claimed duty band is asserted without the necessary condition (middle component fraction).
physics.basis: DWC duty savings scale with the thermodynamic significance of the avoided remixing stream. With no stated feed composition and an α of 1.15 (near-azeotropic behavior making the middle hard to define), the upper bound of the cited 25-35% range is not physically reachable for most plausible feed splits. This is a quantitative wound, not a falsification, but it caps realistic savings at maybe 10-18%.

evidence.attack: The cited record cal:kg03:r1 is truncated: "measured 25-35% energy savings for close-boiling ternary separations versus conventi" — the baseline comparator ("conventional") is cut off. The record appears to compare against a conventional two-column sequence, which is the baseline here, so the magnitude may transfer — but only for ternary feeds, which the candidate does not establish. cal:kg03:r2 addresses vapor/liquid split control operability, not duty reduction magnitude. Neither record supports the specific claim of 27-32% for a binary α=1.15 system.
evidence.basis: cal:kg03:r1 truncation removes the feed composition context; cal:kg03:r2 is about operability windows, not energy savings magnitude. The evidence supports DWC for ternary splits; it does not validate the binary-with-α=1.15 case.

prior_art.attack: cal:kg03:pa1 (cryogenic air separation DWC) and cal:kg03:pa2 (heat-integrated distillation sequences with heat pumps/double-effect) are prior art but neither teaches the exact intervention+mechanism+effect triplet for a specialty-chemical close-boiling solvent split. pa1 is in a different duty regime (cryogenic, different thermodynamics, different scale). pa2 uses a different energy-saving mechanism (heat integration, not internal thermal coupling via a wall). Neither is a mechanism-killing prior-art hit.

boundary_conditions.attack: The stated lower turndown limit is 40%. Many specialty-chemical solvent recovery trains operate at 30-60% turndown due to batch upstream operations and campaign changes. Operation below 40% "degrades vapor split control" — but more critically, at low turndown the dividing wall's hydraulic balance collapses, liquid maldistribution can flood the prefractionator side, and the energy advantage disappears or reverses. The candidate does not specify the operating window of the actual plant; if the plant routinely operates below 40%, the retrofit is non-viable for a large fraction of operating hours, undermining the payback calculation.

experiment_design.attack: The killer experiment specifies a 300 mm pilot with the actual solvent system at identical product specs, measuring duty vs the existing train. This is a genuine, falsifiable test: if measured duty reduction <15% at spec, the mechanism fails economically. The design can kill the candidate. However, the pilot operates isobarically and steady-state; it does not address turndown behavior, fouling on the dividing wall (the boundary explicitly excludes "high-fouling service"), or long-term operability. So the experiment is good for the steady-state duty claim but leaves operational risks untested. Still, this is a real kill-switch on the central claim.

Underwood-Gilliland is a shortcut method for conventional columns and does not contain a "remixing term" that a DWC configuration removes. The actual DWC minimum energy is computed via the Petlyuk equivalent with three Underwood equations coupled by the vapor split ratio. The candidate's equation is notationally plausible but physically undefined — it cannot be evaluated, so the 3.5-year payback number is unsupported by any computable formalism.
equations.basis: Underwood-Gilliland is a column-shortcut method, not a DWC design method. DWC minimum duty requires the Petlyuk/FID formulation (three coupled Underwood equations with RV as a free parameter), not a single f(α, z, splits). The cited equation is a placeholder, not a calculation.

The capex is almost certainly understated by 1.5-3×, pushing payback to 5-10 years and breaking the 3.5-year claim.
economics.basis: DWC retrofits in specialty-chemical service require new structured packing on both wall sides, modified shell (wall welding, manways for wall access per the boundary condition acknowledging cleaning needs), new control valves for vapor/liquid split manipulation, and tie-in downtime. Industry references (e.g., BASF/Linde published DWC retrofit costs) place such projects at multiples of the implied capex envelope. The payback formula's denominator is correct; the numerator is fictional.

mechanism.attack: The mechanism claims capillary rise of 0.3-0.5 m in fine sand drives the entire system, but ignores that a functioning root zone self-regulates at field capacity only when the wick's hydraulic conductivity K(ψ) at the operating matric potential exceeds crop transpiration demand per unit area. For a mature tomato canopy at peak summer ET (~7 mm/day, ~7 L/m²/day), the upward flux through a fine sand wick at ψ near its air-entry value is on the order of 0.1-1 mm/day per unit gradient — orders of magnitude short of demand without an impractically steep gradient. The candidate's own boundary condition concedes this ("crop water demand above the wick's conductance saturates the bed and needs supplemental top watering"), which contradicts the predicted 20-30% cut. Either the physics is wrong or the headline number is.

A system that needs supplemental overhead watering cannot simultaneously deliver "40-60% reduction in foliar wetting events."

boundary_conditions.attack: The candidate admits (a) capillary lift is capped at ~0.5 m, (b) demand above wick conductance requires supplemental top watering, and (c) salts accumulate and need periodic flush. Condition (c) is fatal for closed-loop recirculation but is hand-waved as "periodic flush" — periodic flush of saline water is itself a water-cost line item that the predicted 20-30% cut does not account for. In arid greenhouse operations where the buyer sits, reservoir EC can rise to crop-damaging levels within 2-4 weeks; flush volume plus the supplemental top-watering volume can fully erode the predicted savings.
boundary_conditions.basis: Salt mass balance in a closed subirrigation reservoir: for irrigation water at EC 1.5 dS/m supplying 7 L/m²/day to a tomato crop transpiring ~95% of inputs, salt input to reservoir ≈ salt delivered minus crop uptake; documented EC doubling within 2-4 weeks in recirculating systems (e.g., closed hydroponic literature) means flush events of 10-30% of applied volume are routine. This is not netted against the 20-30% savings claim.

equations.attack: The h_capillary equation (Jurin's law) gives the maximum static rise height, not the steady-state upward flux at a given height. The candidate uses it as if it characterizes system throughput, but K(ψ) for fine sand at ψ approaching the air-entry value is on the order of 10⁻⁶ to 10⁻⁷ m/s — flux through a 0.4 m wick under a small matric head is mm/day, not the L/m²/day the bed must deliver. The E_applied = E_transpiration + E_evaporation_surface equation is a mass balance tautology that does not prove percolation is "removed"; it assumes the wick barrier is impermeable from below, which a saturated sand wick over a free-water reservoir is not — water will leak downward wherever roots do not consume it.
equations.basis: Jurin's law gives h_max = 2σcosθ/(ρgr), valid at equilibrium with zero flux; at finite flux the operating height is much lower. For r ≈ 100 μm fine sand pores, h_max ≈ 0.15 m, already below the stated 0.3-0.5 m operational range. Equation cannot justify stated performance.

predicted_effect.attack: 20-30% applied-water cut is asserted without specifying baseline scheduling (timer-based overhead typically wastes 25-35% to percolation per the candidate's own problem statement, so even a perfect system only nets ~30% — and subirrigation is not perfect, as boundary conditions concede). Yield parity within 5% is unsupported by any cited trial on tomato/cucumber at commercial scale with this specific 40 cm sand wick geometry.
predicted_effect.basis: The effect numbers are not decomposable: foliar-wetting reduction requires zero overhead events, but boundary conditions admit overhead supplementation under high demand. Internal arithmetic is inconsistent.

With bed-to-bed variance in greenhouse trials typically 10-20% for yield and 15-25% for applied water (well-documented in irrigation research), six beds cannot resolve an 8% yield difference at reasonable statistical power (n=6 paired, α=0.05, power=0.8, requires effect size > ~1.0 SD, i.e., >~15% to detect 8%). scalability_manufacturability.basis: Capex vs water-savings arithmetic for the stated buyer (water-scarce but typically not high-cost greenhouse vegetable regions); does not account for sand specification, float-valve maintenance, reservoir lining, or production downtime.

mechanism.attack: The mechanism chain assumes the separation line migrates cleanly onto the 12-15° angled panels and stays attached along their full 0.5-0.7 m extent. On a bluff-bodied van the trailing edge is a sharp 90° vertical corner; turbulent separation at a sharp edge is effectively fixed by geometry, not by upstream pressure gradient. At only 12-15° taper the effective local Reynolds number on the panel and the absence of a fillet at the panel-to-body joint guarantee that separation will re-attach at the rear vertical edge of the panel and roll up into a wake nearly as broad as the original. The claim that Cp recovers from -0.25 toward -0.05 ignores that base pressure is set by the near-wake recirculation zone cross-section, which is governed primarily by the projected base area, not by a shallow aft ramp. A 12-15° boat-tail is below the threshold where meaningful wake contraction occurs (literature on Ahmed-style and production-car boat-tails shows taper angles need to exceed ~20-25° before Cd_base drops measurably). Predicted Cd_base reduction on the order implied is inconsistent with the geometry.
mechanism.basis: 12-15° taper is below the ~20-25° threshold established in bluff-body boat-tail literature for measurable wake contraction; sharp-edge separation at the panel's trailing vertical edge fixes the near-wake geometry regardless of ramp angle. Residence time in the strong-field zone is microseconds. Magnets also lose ~1–2% of remanence per year (NdFeB thermal/magnetic aging), degrading any marginal effect.
